advances: The proposed all-target tradeoff is false. The following complete globally extendable tables have an exact centered-energy formula at every target, including every boundary face, and their displayed maximum divided by \(W/2^n\) tends to zero. A uniform integer interval removes the heavy-atom escape. It does not remove the energy at the Boolean sites, because those sites are interior points of the larger support box. This counterexample concerns the registered tradeoff and does not assert a disproof of the locked weak Oertel conjecture.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. All extensions, face supports, centered laws, energies, halfspace bounds, and limiting estimates are proved directly above.
proof:
The denominator defining \(\varepsilon_k\) exceeds its numerator, since \(k^3-k-2>0\) for \(k\ge2\). Thus \(0<\varepsilon_k<1\). The convex hull of \(D_k\) is exactly \(P_k\), since all vertices of this box belong to \(D_k\). In particular the support is complete in the original ambient lattice.

For \((x,s)\in P_k\), define the convex function
\(V_k(x,s)=t_k\max\{0,-x_1,\ldots,-x_k,x_1-1,\ldots,x_k-1\}\).
Its values at lattice sites are zero when \(x\in\{0,1\}^k\), and \(t_k\) at every other site of \(D_k\). Indeed, every coordinate of such a site is one of \(-1,0,1,2\); the displayed maximum is zero exactly for the Boolean sites and is one otherwise. The function equal to \(e^{-V_k}\) on \(P_k\) and zero outside \(P_k\) is finite-valued and globally log-concave. For two points in \(P_k\), the log-concavity inequality follows from convexity of \(V_k\); if either endpoint lies outside \(P_k\), its required right side is zero. This extension agrees with the specified table at every lattice point, including every zero outside \(D_k\). It also proves convex-admissibility of the canonical potential.

There are \(2^k\) Boolean sites and \(4^k-2^k\) other base sites in each interval slice. There are \(k\) interval sites, proving \(W_k=k(2^k+T_k)\). The original table is invariant under each reflection \(u_i\mapsto1-u_i\), and it is uniform in the last coordinate. Its original mean is therefore \((1/2,\ldots,1/2,(k-1)/2)\), which is not an integer point. No centering assumption on that original law is used below.

We first identify all minimal faces and their intrinsic lattices. The minimal face of a box containing a site fixes exactly those coordinates of the site that equal an endpoint of the corresponding box interval. Every remaining coordinate runs through its whole box interval. Thus, if \(\mathbf j\in\{0,1\}^k\), all first \(k\) coordinates remain free, and
\(F_{(\mathbf j,\ell)}=[-1,2]^k\times F_\ell\), where \(F_\ell=\{\ell\}\) at an endpoint \(\ell\in\{0,k-1\}\), and \(F_\ell=[0,k-1]\) otherwise. If \(\mathbf j\notin\{0,1\}^k\), at least one of its base coordinates is \(-1\) or \(2\), and that coordinate is fixed at that endpoint throughout its minimal face. After translating the fixed coordinates by their integer values, projection to the free coordinates identifies the whole intrinsic lattice with \(\mathbb Z^{\dim F_{\mathbf J}}\). The complete face support is the product of all integer sites in its free coordinate intervals. No sublattice or index factor is introduced.

On a finite interval of consecutive integers \(a,\ldots,b\), the law proportional to \(z^s\), for \(z>0\), has a mean that is continuous and strictly increasing as a function of \(\log z\) when \(a<b\). Its derivative is its strictly positive variance, and its limits are \(a\) and \(b\). Hence every target strictly between the endpoints has a unique positive tilt with that mean. At an endpoint the minimal face is a singleton, whose only probability law is its unit atom. These observations supply all the univariate uniform tilts used below, with every site of its minimal face retained.

If \(\mathbf j\notin\{0,1\}^k\), its minimal face has a fixed exterior base coordinate. Every site on that face consequently has weight \(\varepsilon_k\) and potential \(t_k\). The original weights on that face are constant. The product of the preceding univariate uniform tilts, with unit atoms in fixed coordinates, is a positive Gibbs law on the entire face support with mean \((\mathbf j,\ell)\). Its energy is exactly \(t_k-t_k=0\). This includes all vertices and every face with any fixed exterior base coordinate.

It remains to compute the centered law when the base target is Boolean. First take the base target \(\mathbf0\). For \(x>0\), put

\[
\begin{aligned}
Z_k(x)
&=\sum_{\mathbf u\in\{-1,0,1,2\}^k}
w_{(\mathbf u,0)}x^{u_1+\cdots+u_k}\\
&=(1-\varepsilon_k)(1+x)^k
+\varepsilon_k(x^{-1}+1+x+x^2)^k\\
&=(1+x)^k
\left[1-\varepsilon_k+\varepsilon_k(x+x^{-1})^k\right].
\end{aligned}
\]

The second equality writes the table as a constant \(1-\varepsilon_k\) on the Boolean cube plus a constant \(\varepsilon_k\) on the whole larger cube. All of these are the original weights. Let the base probability of \(\mathbf u\) be
\(w_{(\mathbf u,0)}x^{u_1+\cdots+u_k}/Z_k(x)\), and evaluate it at \(x=1/k\). Define the mixture coefficient

\[
\rho_k
=\frac{\varepsilon_k(k+k^{-1})^k}
{1-\varepsilon_k+\varepsilon_k(k+k^{-1})^k}
=\frac{k^2+1}{(k-1)(k+1)^2}.
\]

For the last equality, direct substitution gives
\(\frac{\varepsilon_k}{1-\varepsilon_k}(k+k^{-1})^k
=(k^2+1)/(k^3-k-2)\), and
\(k^3-k-2+k^2+1=(k-1)(k+1)^2\).
Permutation symmetry makes all base coordinate means equal. Differentiating the finite positive partition sum gives their common value as

\[
\begin{aligned}
\left.\frac{xZ_k'(x)}{kZ_k(x)}\right|_{x=1/k}
&=\frac1{k+1}
-\rho_k\frac{k^2-1}{k^2+1}\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus this is an exactly centered positive Gibbs law on the entire base support, with tilt \((-\log k,\ldots,-\log k)\). The coefficient \(\rho_k\) is the mixture weight of the whole larger-cube term, rather than the probability of being outside the Boolean cube. That latter probability is exactly

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\varepsilon_k\left[(x^{-1}+1+x+x^2)^k-(1+x)^k\right]}{Z_k(x)}
\bigg|_{x=1/k}\\
&\qquad=\rho_k\left[1-(k+k^{-1})^{-k}\right]
=\rho_k\left[1-\left(\frac{k}{k^2+1}\right)^k\right].
\end{aligned}
\]

The potential at the target is zero and is \(t_k\) precisely outside the Boolean cube. This proves the stated value \(G_k\) of its centered energy.

For any other Boolean target \(\mathbf j\), reflect coordinate \(i\) by \(u_i\mapsto1-u_i\) exactly when \(j_i=1\). This maps \(\mathbf j\) to \(\mathbf0\) and preserves the full base support, its original weights, and its potential. Transporting the law just constructed gives a positive Gibbs law with mean \(\mathbf j\) and the same energy \(G_k\). Its tilt in coordinate \(i\) is \(-\log k\) when \(j_i=0\), and \(+\log k\) when \(j_i=1\).

On the full minimal face \([-1,2]^k\times F_\ell\), multiply this base law by the univariate uniform tilt on \(F_\ell\cap\mathbb Z\) with mean \(\ell\). The original face weights factor as the original base weights times the constant interval weights. The resulting product is therefore a Gibbs tilt of exactly the original face weights and is positive at every site of that face. Its mean is \((\mathbf j,\ell)\). Since the potential is independent of the interval coordinate, its energy remains \(G_k\), including at both interval endpoints.

For completeness, all the centered Gibbs laws just exhibited are the unique centered optimizing laws on their face supports. On the whole intrinsic coordinate space of a positive-dimensional face, the Hessian of the log partition sum is its covariance matrix. It is positive definite because all sites of a support spanning that space have positive probability: a nonzero linear functional cannot be constant on that support. Thus the gradient, which is the mean, takes a specified value at at most one tilt. In rank zero the law is the unit atom. This proves both uniqueness and the exact energy formula at every target without replacing any face by a selected support.

We now bound the actual original marginal depths by explicit closed halfspaces. Fix a Boolean base target \(\mathbf j\), and let \(a_i=2j_i-1\). For any \(\mathbf u\in\{0,1\}^k\),
\(\sum_i a_i(u_i-j_i)\) is minus the number of coordinates where \(\mathbf u\) differs from \(\mathbf j\). Consequently the proper closed halfspace

\[
H_{\mathbf j}
=\left\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:
\sum_{i=1}^k a_i(x_i-j_i)\ge0\right\}
\]

contains \((\mathbf j,\ell)\) for every interval target \(\ell\), and contains exactly the one Boolean row with base \(\mathbf j\). That row has original mass \(k\). Every other included site belongs to the surrounding part, whose entire original mass is \(kT_k\). Thus
\(\tau_{(\mathbf j,\ell)}\le k(1+T_k)\) at every Boolean base target. All equality atoms in this closed halfspace are included in that bound.

If \(\mathbf j\notin\{0,1\}^k\), choose an exterior coordinate. When \(j_i=-1\), the closed halfspace \(\{(x,s):x_i\le-1\}\) contains the target; when \(j_i=2\), use \(\{(x,s):x_i\ge2\}\). In either case it contains exactly \(4^{k-1}\) base sites in each interval slice, all of original weight \(\varepsilon_k\). Its original mass is \(k\varepsilon_k4^{k-1}\). Hence
\(\tau_{(\mathbf j,\ell)}\le k\varepsilon_k4^{k-1}\) at every non-Boolean base target. These cases exhaust all targets and every boundary face.

Since \(W_k\ge k2^k\), \(w_{\mathbf J}\le1\), and the two target classes have respective energies \(G_k\) and zero, the preceding halfspaces give

\[
\frac{2^{k+1}}{W_k}
\max_{\mathbf J\in D_k}
\max\left\{w_{\mathbf J},\frac{\tau_{\mathbf J}}{1+g_{\mathbf J}}\right\}
\le
\max\left\{\frac2k,
\frac{2(1+T_k)}{1+G_k},
2\varepsilon_k4^{k-1}\right\}.
\]

Finally,
\(k^3-k-2-k^2=(k-2)(k^2+k+1)\ge0\).
The denominator of \(\varepsilon_k\) is therefore at least \(k^{2k}\), so \(\varepsilon_k\le k^{-k}\) and \(t_k\ge k\log k\). Also
\(\rho_k\ge1/(k+1)\), and
\((k/(k^2+1))^k\le k^{-k}\le1/4\).
In particular

\[
G_k\ge\frac{k\log k}{2(k+1)}\ge\frac{\log k}{3},
\qquad
T_k\le(4/k)^k,
\qquad
2\varepsilon_k4^{k-1}\le\frac12(4/k)^k.
\]

Substitution gives the final explicit upper bound in the statement. Each of its three terms tends to zero. For every proposed absolute \(c>0\), a sufficiently large \(k\) therefore makes the original displayed maximum strictly less than \(cW_k/2^{k+1}\). This proves the claimed all-target disproof.
